titleStmt.title: Memorandum From Secretary of State Shultz to President Reagan

div.head: 375. Memorandum From Secretary of State Shultz to President Reagan

list.label: SUBJECT
list.item: Official Working Visit of President Osvaldo Hurtado of Ecuador

div.p: President Hurtado visits Washington at the most troubled time since Ecuador returned to democracy in 1979. Economic activity is at its lowest level in years and has fueled discontent with the government in business, labor and military sectors. Hurtado’s courageous decision in March to impose essential austerity measures needed to come to terms with the IMF prompted a potentially dangerous general strike. U.S. political support has been important to Hurtado. He very much wanted and welcomed the White House invitation. (He was scheduled for a visit in May 1982 but requested a postponement because of the South Atlantic conflict.)

Democracy’s roots in Ecuador are tender but Hurtado is dedicated to nurturing them. As a scholar and leader of the left-of-center Christian Democrats, his hope has been to wean Ecuador away from destructive cycles of personalism and militarism. His party’s minority position and the financial emergency, however, have hampered his efforts. Since mid-1982, his main goal has been to see Ecuador through to the elections in 1984.

The President draws some strength from the democratic structure he is trying to preserve. Most politicians and influential newspapers still back the constitutional order. Despite political unrest, Ecuador remains free of guerrillas and terrorists. Moderate military leaders realize they have no better proposals for dealing with the economic crisis than do the civilians. Helpful, too, have been the patience and understanding of foreign banks. Finally, widespread awareness that the U.S. and other hemispheric democracies would not look kindly on a coup has restrained plotters.

Hurtado faces formidable problems. Unfulfilled hopes raised by the oil wealth of the seventies haunt the country. Inflation, now 30 percent, pinches the man on the street. The business community is troubled and distrusts the President’s motives. The congress avoids responsibility for painful economic measures. Unions sometimes press unreasonable demands.

Some military leaders are restive and ambitious; even those who are not brood about the impact of the economic crisis on military income and hardware procurement. Should the armed forces not intervene effectively on Hurtado’s behalf in case of sustained popular unrest, the government could fall.

Hurtado’s style contributes to his troubles. Formerly the Vice President, he was thrust unexpectedly into the limelight when President Roldos died in an aircraft accident in 1981. He is thoughtful, rather remote, and ill at ease with political infighting in a society which expects flamboyance and demagoguery from its leaders. While respected for his personal integrity and honesty, his seeming immobility in the face of difficult decisions leads to accusations of indecision.

We want to demonstrate our strong commitment to Ecuador’s democratic system to Hurtado’s allies and adversaries and to the hemisphere as a whole. The U.S. already has played a key role through public support at nervous moments, visits of senior U.S. officials, CCC credits, the recent lifting of our tuna embargo and, most importantly, in the Presidential invitation.

We have told the Ecuadoreans not to expect additional economic assistance from this trip, but they will probably seek greater support in dealing with their current problems and with hemisphere debt problems generally. We should commend Hurtado’s efforts to reach agreement with the IMF and indicate our willingness to convey to the commercial banks our support for his economic reform program.

Our relations are generally excellent. Our economic and security assistance is modest but welcome. The Ecuadoreans are seeking reconsideration of the recent increase in Panama Canal tolls. Central America is not a major concern in Ecuador but the visit is a good opportunity to relate our strategy to Hurtado’s interest in hemisphere security. We should avoid any attempts to draw us into Ecuador’s historic dispute with Peru over access to the Amazon.

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, George P. Shultz Papers, Box 28E, Latin America. Confidential. Drafted on March 18 by Scott; cleared in ARA/PPC, ARA/ECP, P/M, S/P, P, EB/FD/OMA, E, OES, AID/LAC/SA, IO/UNP, INR, and INM/P. Enders sent the memorandum to Shultz under cover of a March 30 memorandum in which he wrote: “Hurtado’s working visit affords us the opportunity to reinforce our generally good bilateral relations with Ecuador; there are no urgently pressing issues in dispute.” See Document 376 and footnote 1 thereto.

Reagan’s May 4, 1982, letter inviting Hurtado for a June 21–23, 1982, working visit is in the Reagan Library, Executive Secretariat, NSC Country File, Latin America/Central, Ecuador (03/29/1983–11/01/1983).

In telegram 3865 from Quito, June 2, 1982, the Embassy reported on the cancellation of Ecuador’s participation in military exercise UNITAS XXIII and of Hurtado’s U.S. trip describing the later as a “last minute decision” and that “his decision was later explained to us by Foreign Ministry as taken reluctantly—out of a desire not to expose himself to press questions, at this juncture, on the South Atlantic crisis which could embarrass U.S.-Ecuadorean relations, either through adverse domestic reaction or by giving offense to U.S. hosts.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D820290–0522)

In telegram 33460 to Quito, February 4, the Department wrote: “Dept. agrees with Ambassador that conditions now permit the U.S. to lift the embargo on Ecuadorean tuna products imposed in 1980” and instructed the Embassy to seek Ecuadorean participation in a regional licensing agreement. “In sum, Embassy may advise appropriate GOE officials that the USG is now willing to remove the embargo against Ecuadorean tuna products and is preparing the paperwork necessary to accomplish this, but that we do not want any public announcement concerning embargo at this time.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D830066–0222) The “Removal of Prohibition on Importation of Tuna and Tuna Products From Ecuador and Peru,” was published by the Customs Service in the Federal Register, vol. 48, No. 76, April, 19, 1983, pp. 16798–16799.
